q: List FortiWeb's operation modes. For the two transparent modes (TTP and TI), how do they differ in traffic modification, HTTPS handling, TLS support, and user authentication?
kp: Operation modes: Reverse Proxy, True Transparent Proxy (TTP), Transparent Inspection (TI), WCCP, Offline Protection
TTP: full security features, can modify traffic (header insertion, error pages), decrypts and re-encrypts HTTPS, supports TLS 1.0/1.1/1.2/1.3, supports user authentication
TI: limited security features, does not modify traffic, can decrypt HTTPS but does not re-encrypt, supports TLS 1.0/1.1/1.2 but not TLS 1.3, no user authentication
Both are Layer 2 bridge modes where traffic is inspected at the bridge interface without changing the destination IP address (server responds directly)

q: How does FortiWeb apply its protection profile scans (the 'sequence of scans')? Name the first few scans/actions in order, and what happens when a source IP is in the allow list?
kp: Scans are applied in the order of the scan sequence table, read top to bottom (first scan/action to last); disabled scans are skipped

Early scans/actions include: adding X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP/X-Forwarded-Proto headers, IP List, TCP Connection Number Limit (TCP flood prevention), IP Reputation, Quarantined source IP addresses, Known Bots, Geo IP
If a source IP is allow listed, subsequent checks will be skipped
Performance guidance: block attackers using the earliest possible technique and/or the least memory-consuming technique

q: Describe the two-layer approach of FortiWeb's Machine Learning based Anomaly Detection, and explain the difference between the 'standard' and 'extended' svm-type options.
kp: First layer: Hidden Markov Model (HMM) monitors and builds a model of normal application behavior, flagging deviating requests as potential anomalies
Second layer: verifies the anomalies using pre-built, continuously updated threat models trained on thousands of real attack samples (e.g. SQL injection, XSS)
svm-type standard (default): system automatically disables SVM models which can easily trigger false positives
svm-type extended: enables all SVM models

q: What does FortiWeb HA heartbeat traffic use (address/port), how is heartbeat timeout calculated, and what does the standby appliance do when the active one fails?
kp: Heartbeat uses multicast on port 6065 and IP address 239.0.0.1; HA IP addresses are hard-coded and cannot be modified
Heartbeat timeout = Detection Interval x Heartbeat Lost Threshold
On failure the standby assumes the virtual MAC address of the failed primary and broadcasts ARP/NS packets so network equipment refreshes MAC forwarding tables
Standby then assumes the active role and scans network traffic; switches/routers on heartbeat interfaces must allow level 2 frames

q: What are the requirements and traffic-distribution behavior of FortiWeb High Volume Active-Active HA mode?
kp: Only available in Reverse Proxy operation mode
Supports up to eight FortiWeb appliances
Does not rely on a central primary appliance to distribute traffic; each HA member is assigned one or more unique virtual IPs (VIPs) that directly receive and process traffic
On failure, a designated backup appliance assumes responsibility for the affected virtual IPs

q: How is the maximum number of server policies on a FortiWeb-VM determined by vRAM, and how many virtual network interfaces does FortiWeb-VM have?
kp: FortiWeb-VM has 10 virtual network interfaces (vNICs)
vRAM less than 64 GB: up to 20 server policies for the first 1 GB of vRAM, then +15 policies per additional 1 GB, up to a maximum of 256 server policies
vRAM of 64 GB or more: up to 1024 server policies
vRAM is taken from MemTotal of 'diagnose hardware mem list', KB rounded down to integer GB

q: In Active-Passive and standard Active-Active HA modes, how do you manage the secondary FortiWeb node via SSH or GUI, and what virtual MAC behavior applies in these modes?
kp: Add a reserved management interface (set the port as Reserved Management Interface) so its IP/settings are not synchronized to other HA members, plus an HA static/policy route to reach the secondary node
Not strictly required for HA setup but necessary for managing secondary nodes in active-passive and standard active-active modes

In Active-Passive and Active-Active-Standard modes, traffic ports and VIPs on the primary use a virtual MAC address (format like 00:09:0F:A0:CC:02); secondary nodes use their real MAC until they become primary

q: What is FortiWeb Manager (FWM) used for? Name at least four management functions it provides.
kp: FWM centrally manages multiple FortiWeb appliances
Managing FortiWeb devices: adding device groups, adding devices, upgrading devices
Managing FortiWeb-VM licenses (applying and reclaiming VM licenses)
Jobs: scheduled tasks with job status notification
Monitoring FortiWeb devices and viewing logs; API proxy support

q: How do you enable FortiWeb traffic log storage on the appliance hard disk via CLI, what permission is needed, and why must it be handled with care?
kp: CLI: config log traffic-log / set disk-log enable
Requires an account with 'w' or 'rw' permission on the loggrp area
In most environments, especially high traffic volume, enabling disk logging for long periods can cause the hard disk to fail prematurely - disable as soon as not needed
Verify with 'get log traffic-log'; sample messages with 'diagnose log tlog show'

q: How is web caching (WCCP) enabled and matched on FortiWeb, and what happens when multiple web cache rules exist in one policy?
kp: Enable Web Cache in System > Config > Feature Visibility
Enabling Web Cache on an HTTP server policy (Policy > Server Policy) automatically creates a web cache policy in Application Delivery > Caching
A web cache rule is required, otherwise the web cache policy will not match
Multiple rules are matched in order: when the first rule matches, the remaining rules are skipped and do not take effect
